cues.en: In this lecture, I want to give you an overview about additional features that llVM supports.
The reason is that if you want to use llVM in production, there are way more features available and
you might consider using some of those.

it works and that you can consider whether this is something appropriate for the project or whether
you want to avoid using it.

So I can't offer you that as a chapter here, but I would like to mention a few additional features
so that you are aware of them that they do exist in llVM.
The first thing that I would like to mention is that llVM can be run on top of a raid.
Raid stands for redundant array of independent disks and the idea for the raid exists in hardware raids
and software raids.
Whether it's something that our operating system manages or something that our hardware managers.
But we can run that on top of a software raid, for example.
And there are different raid flavors available or configurations, for example, Raid zero it's called
it's just does striping that one file is split to multiple disks.
So if it's split to multiple disks, we can read parts of that file there.
Like one part of that file is on the first disk.
The next part is on the next disk and so on.
So it increases our performance because we can read from from multiple disks at the same time.
But if one of our physical disks would fail, then we have a problem because we can't recover the data.
But that would be a raid zero that configuration.
Or we could also have a raid.
Five It also uses striping that the data is stored on different disks.
But we also store so-called parity bits.
And this will allow that one drive can fail and we can still recover all the data.
Or there's also Raid six.
This means that we lose the storage space of two drives, but that means that two drives can fail.
And we do have some redundancy here.
It means, by the way, if I have written there, two drives can fail.
It means that any of the drives can fail.
So we can just pick two that fail and it will still work.
I don't want to talk too much about Raid because that's another topic, but we have seen how pretty
much llVM was just accessing our block devices and whether the block device is like a partition or whether
that's a raid.
It doesn't really matter for llVM.
So llVM is a great way to run a raid.
Another thing that I would like to mention is that llVM also supports so-called thin volumes.

logical volume on top.

But as long as we realize that ahead of time, we could just add additional drives later and extend
our of our volume group and then everything should work and this would be a thin volume.
Another feature is that we can use snapshots so we can say, Hey, we want to create a snapshot.

It just says, Hey, we have now created a snapshot.
If data is changed after the snapshot, it will need to be rewritten because we can't lose that snapshot,
but only if data is changed after the snapshot.
We actually need space for that snapshot.
So the snapshot itself is extremely small, only the changes that come after.
Of course we need to uh, store them separately.
Then.
Um, the idea here is that this allows us, for example, in a setup to create a snapshot of our drive
without turning off anything, our computer can still be running.
Then we can copy the snapshot as a backup.
It will be consistent because it will represent a specific point in time of our file system, but at
the same time, our computer can keep running and it can do the next tasks already.
Again, if changes to our file system happen, we will need more storage then for those changes.
But the snapshot itself will remain intact and will remain consistent.
And this allows us to create a snapshot, Copy that snapshot as a backup, and then we can just remove
that snapshot again.
And we have a consistent backup solution that can back up a specific point in time for the whole file

Aside from of course, if the drives are working, it might not be beneficial for the performance of
our applications.
But aside from that, we do have the ability to create consistent snapshots and this can be extremely
